The Data Recipient agrees to process the Data only for the following purposes agreed with the HSCIC: 
Objective for processing:  
Harvey Walsh is an IT solutions, NHS Informatics and Healthcare Consultancy which provides services to the NHS, Pharmaceutical and Device Industry, Patient Groups and Healthcare Charities.  
Harvey Walsh uses pseudonymised, monthly refreshed HES data to undertake analysis, develop services and provide solutions to support commissioning for NHS organisations, which includes GP Practices, CCGs, LATs, AHSNs, Health and Well-Being Boards, Provider Trusts, Ambulance Trusts and CSUs. The services and solutions provided include access to a secure on-line system called Axon, data is presented through three views (varying depending upon the nature of the organisation accessing the data) namely AXON Data Manager, AXON Profiler and AXON Analyser. Data is also analysed for the purposes of informing commissioners, clinicians and clinical networks on uptake on innovation, national policy guidelines, including NICE, patient pathways, benchmarking and disease burden analytics. The insights and analysis may be on a national level or down to individual practice level.
Harvey Walsh also utilize these HES data to provide services to commercial organisations within the pharmaceutical, medical device industry and patient organisations. These organization use the outputs and insights to work collaboratively with NHS organisations to promote health and improve the wellbeing of patients. The use of the data supports the development of innovative solutions and service improvement, to track outcomes and provide the real world evidence as required by the NHS, NICE, Monitor and NHS England .  The aim of which is to improve patient care and support enhanced access to improved services and innovative solutions.  In additional these clients also access data held within AXON for the purposes of providing supporting information required by the NHS for  business cases, epidemiological research, pathway analysis, burden of disease analysis, health economic research, NICE submissions and quality and outcome analysis. The outputs of which are shared directly with the NHS to support improvements in patient care
The outputs and systems that utilize the HES data are provided in two ways: directly to the NHS via AXON or indirectly to the NHS via pharmaceutical and device companies using outputs, reports, dashboards and  research papers produced by Harvey Walsh. ALL of the outputs from the analysis of HES are used directly or indirectly for the provision or promotion of health and improved patient care and are not wholly commercial.

Processing activities and Methodology:
Harvey Walsh have received data on a monthly basis for the past 4 years. These data are received by secure FTP and loaded into a data warehouse called AXON which is owned and managed wholly by Harvey Walsh. The data are processed and aggregated as per HSCIC guidance. The data are processed using methodology which allows for a large and varied set of metrics to be produced dependent on the project or output being undertaken. This includes trend analysis, risk stratification, cohort and pathway mapping which can be used to demonstrate geographical variances, burden of disease costs and benchmarking of organisations against pathways and national targets. Analysis of organisations against multiple diseases, pathways and referrals to secondary care. Linked pathway analysis utilizing the unique HESID is also undertaken to evaluate the full pathway between inpatient, outpatient and A&E.
These data are processed on a on-line systems which are securely hosted on dedicated servers and access provided via secure log on.  The data are held within a data warehouse called AXON, and presently data is presented through three views (varying depending upon the nature of the organisation accessing the data) namely AXON Data Manager, AXON Profiler and AXON Analyser.  All data are aggregated at organisational level within the data warehouse and small numbers are suppressed.
No record level data is provided to any third party organisation in any format.  
No data is used for direct marketing to individuals.
No data is used to direct  sales activities.
An example of how these processed data are used: The HES data may be analysed for a specific patient cohort for example in Atrial Fibrillation. A pathway utilization would be developed for patients flowing through the system linking the healthcare utilization costs of inpatient, outpatient and A&E activity on a geographical basis. This analysis would then be used to populate a pathway model which would be used by a Pharmaceutical company in conjunction with a commissioner/healthcare professional. To identify variations in care and support the CCG/Provider in developing care pathways which improve the detection, management and referrals for patients for these conditions.
The data warehouse does contain other organisational level data  (eg: GP Level Prescribing data and other freely available Open Data), which is combined to form the aggregate views for customers. 
These data are securely stored in a data warehouse called AXON and processed in one location in England by a team of NHS Data Analysts and Health Economists. These data are processed under IS027001/2013, NHS IG Toolkit and Data Protection Act rules and regulations. No record level or aggregated data are transferred, stored or processed outside of the UK. 
Specific outputs expected, including target date:
Harvey Walsh undertake numerous projects utilizing HES on a yearly basis, approximately 80 distinct projects were completed in 2014. The outputs are varied and in different format ranging from reports, charts, dashboards, budget impact models, health economic models, system dynamic models, health economic analysis, risk stratification, variance or via the online system AXON Data Manager, Profiler and Analyser provided either on-line or accessible off-line, research papers and publications, see example at end of document.  
These outputs have achieved many useful things including changes in patient care, reduction in costs, uptake and monitoring of NHS policy. Harvey Walsh have a number of rolling contracts and Harvey Walsh expect to produce outputs on these up until at least 2017.
Any output or analysis is ultimately delivered to directly improve patient care, pathways or healthcare services.
Expected measurable benefits to health and/or social care including target date:
Harvey Walsh has held a data reuse licence for over 7 years and has provided services to the NHS (trusts, CCGs, GP practices) and other healthcare related companies (Pharmaceutical and Device Companies, Patient Groups and Charities) during this time. Harvey Walsh have contracts which run through to 2017 and beyond and would expect to provide HES outputs through to this time.
The solutions and projects that Harvey Walsh undertake have utilized cohort data from 2007 to date, and have been used for numerous different projects.
The benefits that are provided from the analysis and insights of the HES data are direct and indirect to the patient and health and social care environment.
Below are 3 examples of direct benefits to patients and the NHS:
1: In recent years, NICE has issued guidance on the management of Gout. Harvey Walsh undertook research on the burden of Gout for a pharmaceutical client and produced reports and a comparator dashboard. The outputs showed both the prevalence and incidence of gout have increased significantly in the UK with large variations nationally, particularly between the North East and the South East of England. 
The dashboards have been used by the pharmaceutical client in non-promotional meetings with NHS personnel including commissioners, GPs, service managers and consultants to highlight the variance and local burden of Gout. Gout often presents as extreme pain and so patients seek immediate emergency help, often via A&E. resulting in increased costs and avoidable non-elective admissions. These dashboards have resulted in local projects to review the awareness of the management of Gout and outcomes including education to improve the implementation of the NICE guidance and management of patients. HES has been used to track reductions in A&E and non-elective admissions during and after the pathway redesign programmes to produce demonstrable benefits to the local NHS.
In addition longitudinal analysis of the gout HES data also reveals some interesting indicators about the types of patients admitted with gout, for example over 90% of patients admitted with gout go on to be admitted with a cardiac related condition, this insight encouraged GPs to actively review patients with a history of gout.
In this project the use of HES has directly led to improved patient care by increased awareness of Gout, improved education and management which has reduced activity in A&E, emergency admissions to hospital and driven a review of patients with cardiac related conditions. This programme is ongoing and has been used by over 55 CCGs. To date 514 practices have undertaken patient reviews which equates to around 5,500 patients checked for cardiac complications as a result of the intitial HES developed Gout insights dashboard.

2: In 2014 a device company commissioned Harvey Walsh to undertake analysis of Chronic Constipation. Currently Chronic Constipation accounts for over 50,591 non-elective admissions in England in 2014 at a total cost of £63,200, 825 and an average cost of £1249 per spell. Harvey Walsh used longitudinal analysis on the HES data to determine the total healthcare burden and utilisation of patients with constipation and a sub group of patients with constipation and neurogenic bowel disorders. This insights dashboard is used directly by Coloplast with CCGs and Hospital Trusts in evaluating the impact of constipation on a local health economy. To date these outputs and tools have directly resulted in 8 CCGs (3 million approx. population) undertaking pathway analysis projects which include the following activity:
• Baseline assessment and variance to other CCGs through a benchmarking exercise
• Benchmarking of practices with high levels of non-elective admissions
• Targeted education on these practices
• Development of  Chronic Constipation pathways
The use of monthly refreshed HES has led to a direct benefit of improved patient care. Enhanced education and implementation of pathways has resulted in a reduction in the numbers of Non Elective (NEL) admissions (17% reduction in Newcastle), length of stay (5.6 days to 4.3 days), total bed days, and costs bringing an ongoing benefit of HES to the local health economy.
This type of analysis and outcomes has been undertaken in many disease areas not just Constipation with the ultimate aim of improving outcomes for patients and health and social care.
3. In 2014 NHS England commissioned Harvey Walsh to undertake a 2 year programme of analysis using HES on the uptake of Venous Thromboprohylaxis Event (VTE) guidance and Novel Oral Anti Coagulants (NOACS) over the past 3 years to determine the beneficial outcomes of the policy for patients. Harvey Walsh analyzed 7 years of HES data to understand the number of patients having a VTE following hospital admission before NHS guidance was put in place and after the NHS VTE program commenced. These data have been broken down into cohorts including high risk patients, low risk patients, surgical patients, medical patients, patients >60 and <60, patients having orthopedic procedures vs those who have had cardiovascular, oncology or respiratory procedures, and also for those patients admitted non-electively vs electively. 
These outcomes are being used by the VTE team to understand which patient cohorts have responded well to the NHS VTE program and where there needs to be additional focus in the future. It is clear from the initial analysis that some areas including those patients with Hip and knee procedures have had some reductions in the number of patients re-admitting with a VTE post procedure despite the increasing number of patient admissions over the past few years. However there are some areas specifically in non-elective care where the number of patients re-presenting with a VTE post procedure or a stay in hospital have increased. All patients require equity of care. However VTE is a significant burden to the NHS. Working with the team to highlight and understand how this area needs to be managed, monitored and amended in the future is critical to improving outcomes for patients and the NHS, reducing unnecessary patient admissions and increasing capacity for other patient care requirements. 
In addition to this program Harvey Walsh are also working with an NHS trust to understand the effect of VTE in patients receiving cancer care. The outcome of this is to understand how cancer and cancer acquired thrombosis (CAT) have changed over the years and what the burden is in specific cancer types. More than 30% of all VTE patients in England in the year 2011/12 were also being treated for cancer. In addition, 17% of all patients who had a diagnosis of cancer in 2011/12 went on to have a VTE within 1 year of their diagnosis. This project currently being undertaken will enable Healthcare professionals to understand which patients require changes to care pathways specifically around the management of VTE and VTE prophylaxis. 
If the project is to develop further in the future, the health service would benefit from understanding the variation of care for Oncology specifically related to VTE and how areas with best practice can be shared to improve care for patients in areas where there is under-performance. 
The direct benefit of this analysis has been to demonstrate the importance of management of VTEs and the effectiveness of NHS England policy and implementation and to highlight further areas for improvement.
Below are a summary of additional examples of the in-direct and direct benefits to patients and healthcare.

• In January 2014, NICE issued new guideline for the management of Prostate Cancer, these included guidelines on the removal of the prostrate using Robotic Assisted Surgery. It further stated that commissioners should ensure that, where the technique was to be offered that those centres should be performing at least 150 robot assisted laparoscopic radical prostatectomies per year. There was a request to the company that manufactures the Robots to undertake analysis of the current burden and to provide data to support commissioners and business managers in planning services to ensure that the guidance was met and that patients had access to this new technology and to demonstrate the comparison with traditional surgery. 
Analysis of the HES cohort data was undertaken to understand the pathways between robotic and non-robotic surgery. This analysis was commissioning by the manufacturer and undertaken by Harvey Walsh and showed rate of post surgical infection, incontinence, readmissions and length of stay by provider for patients treated with a robotic surgical procedure versus traditional surgical methods. These outputs are accessible and can be provided to all commissioners and providers (free of charge) by the manufacturer and the data is also shared by the clinicians who authored the analysis and will be submitted to NICE as supporting evidence for post guidance outcomes. The outputs which is a health economic model is being used to inform the commissioning strategy for these procedures for hospitals in England and to improve the access to these innovative procedures for patients. In addition an abstract is being produced for disseminations by clinicians at a NHS conference later in 2015.
• Working with a pharmaceutical client, to develop a health economic model to demonstrate the variation of lung cancer diagnosis rates and access to treatment across CCGs and parliamentary constituencies.This model is non-promotional and does not contain reference to or  highlight the drugs provided by the pharmaceutical company. This model is used by non-promotional personnel in non-promotional calls. This model is used in conversations with commissioners and clinicians to highlight the issues of late diagnosis of lung cancer and to demonstrate the variance of care across the UK with the aim of  gaining agreement for the development of collaborative projects with the NHS. The aim of which is to improve the access of patients to earlier diagnosis and access to treatment through the development of enhanced services, education and pathways. These outputs were also used in the House of Commons with MPs so that they were aware of how their patients outcomes may be different to other constituencies.
• The pharmaceutical industry is governed by strict guidelines under the ABPI (Association of British Pharmaceutical Industry) These guidelines dictate how a pharmaceutical company interacts with the NHS. Therefore the majority of Pharmaceutical companies have non-promotional (not sales people). The roles of these teams is to engage (freely and without favour) with the NHS on a national, regional and local level to improve outcomes for patients and promote of health.
The NHS is free to choose who to engage with and no payment is offered or received for this engagement. As part of this engagement the Pharmaceutical clients may use analysis, reports and outputs in the form of models to demonstrate the local, regional and national pathways for diseases. They may also use data from AXON or request access to AXON so that they can engage with commissioners, clinicians and other NHS personnel and have informed discussions on the burden of disease, pathways and outcomes with regards to local and NHS National Policy. Providing these groups with the information they need to make informed decisions about innovation, value and outcomes for patients and services.
No charge is made to the NHS for access to these data and outcomes.
The benefits for the analysis and solutions provided by Harvey Walsh have been recognized directly, for example see email below from Newcastle CCG regarding work that Harvey Walsh has undertaken for the NHS:
“In my role as the CEO of an innovative GP federation which is an aspirant Multi Specialty Community Provider (MCP) I have frequent contact with pharmaceutical and medtech companies that use applied health economic arguments to demonstrate the value of their product. Their ability to do so is often dependent upon the quality of the tools that they use and the integrity of the analysis that underpins those tools. “
“In my experience the Harvey Walsh analysis is far more robust and aligned to NHS characteristics than other approaches; for example in the ability to view by HRG, ICD10, commissioner and provider perspectives. 
Our GP federation is looking to run a range of new services and each one requires extensive business case development. We have approached Harvey Walsh for data and for contextual analysis in particular as their ability to show comparisons is excellent. We also find it useful to have their creative ability to consider different ways of looking to solve complex problems. This is increasingly important as we develop unprecedented and innovative services as the mainstream NHS information reporting tends to be slow, inflexible and set to PbR and other rigid processes. 
Chief Executive
Washington Community Health Care - 
a collaboration of local primary care practices “

Greater Manchester Academic Health Science Network (GMASHN) currently has a work stream regarding Atrial Fibrillation. Harvey Walsh were commissioned by the ASHN to undertake analysis of HES to support this workstream and develop an interactive performance and insights dashboard. Below is a summary supplied by the AHSN on how Harvey Walsh has supported this work and what the aims of the AHSN are.
There are two strong directives that the AHSN has to work in this field, firstly to accelerate the effective adoption of NICE guidelines and secondly when we first got our licence we went to the Association of CCGs to confirm our work programme and priorities in CVD as Atrial Fibrillation, Familial Hypercholesterolaemia and chronic kidney disease. Therefore we are undertaking this on behalf of, and with the consent of our member organisation.
Applying Nice Guidelines CG 180 has the potential to reduce the risk of stroke to 69% of its current level and save approximately 10,000 strokes occurring.
We believe in Greater Manchester we could save a Stroke a day - 365 a year -  a very conservative estimate.
1 in 6 patients with AFhas a stroke and the prevalence of AF is growing by 5% each year currently. 
NICE guidelines identify levels of risk stratification as:-
• AF on no treatment - 28.9%
• AF on Aspirin as a mono therapy - 22&(Aspirin as a mono therapy will not reduce the risk of an AF related stroke)
• Of the remaining patients on an anti-coagulant, Time in Treatment range is critical but difficult to attain for many, QOF achievements although reasonable in many places have an the element of risk around those exception reported too
“We have been successfully working with Harvey Walsh to provide a Data Landscape for each of our CCGs that pull from a range of publically available data sets including HES data into one complete story regarding AF related strokes.
Understanding potential bed days saved include excess ones, A&E admissions etc is part of the health economic and health gains information that galvanises the health community to rise to this challenge.
Best wishes
Associate Director of Nursing and Improvement.”
Health and Implementation.
Hernia surgery is complex and may require many weeks off work for patients who undergo it. Currently there are no national published guidelines and NICE has begun the development of guidelines for publication in 2016. New and innovative surgical techniques have been emerging over the past few years. Commissioners have been reluctant to fund these technologies due to the lack of national guidance and many surgical providers have had to ration access to these treatments due to funding issues. 
Surgeons who use this technology wish to provide evidence to commissioners of the beneficial outcome using MESH technology and as such Harvey Walsh have undertaken analysis of HES in a health economic publication which is shown below. This is an example of how HES data has been used collaboratively between industry and the NHS to improve patient access and improve the provision of innovative care. This abstract has been submitted for publication in the BMJ and will be submitted to NICE. On a local level the analysis is used by surgeons to develop business cases for submission to commissioners to increase the access to these new surgical techniques. The data are not used by sales personnel in sales pitches.
Secondary healthcare resource utilisation following major abdominal surgery employing an acellular reconstructive tissue matrix
Miss S Das Mohapatra, DNB,FRCS(Gen Surg), Consultant Colorectal Surgeon; Mr J O’Hara MSc, Director - Healthcare Decisions; Miss C Camp MSc, Health Economist - Healthcare Decisions; Prof D Hughes PhD, Director - Healthcare Decisions; Mr A C J Windsor MBBS, MD, FRCS, FRCS(Ed) FRCS (Glas), Consultant Colorectal Surgeon.
University College London Hospital, UK; Healthcare Decisions, Cheshire, UK; University of Chester, UK.
Purpose
Evidence supporting the clinical effectiveness of biological mesh in major abdominal surgery, in particular resource use and outcomes post-intervention, remains poor. However, rapid advances in surgical technology combined with increasingly restrictive budgets for healthcare systems means that demand for such evidence is increasing. This study is a preliminary investigation into resource utilisation pre- and post-intervention in major reconstructive surgeries involving the deployment of Strattice™ Reconstructive Tissue Matrix (RTM), an acellular porcine dermal matrix.
Methods
A before-after analysis of secondary healthcare resource utilisation was conducted for 154 major abdominal surgeries undertaken at University College London Hospital (UCLH) between February 2010 and October 2013. All interventions employed Strattice™ RTM. Pre- and post-intervention pathways (inpatient, outpatient, and Accident & Emergency (A&E)) were quantified using Hospital Episode Statistics (HES) covering NHS hospitals in England (data for April 2008 to December 2013). Significance tests for temporal differences in resource use were conducted using a non-parametric paired t-test (Sign test).
Results
Mean age at intervention was 57.5 years (SD 12.9). 54% of those undergoing surgery were female. Three-quarters of interventions occurred as part of an elective admission. The most frequently observed primary diagnosis (ICD-10) at intervention was ventral hernia (31.2%), followed by intestinal fistula (15.3%). During the observed period, Strattice™ RTM was predominantly employed for the repair of incisional hernia (35.7% of interventions).
A total of 11,798 pre- and post-intervention observations were recorded in the sample period. An average of 3.4 years’ worth of data was available prior to intervention; the average follow-up period was 2.4 years.
Inpatient spell frequency decreased by an average of 2.0 admissions (SD 12.7; p<0.001) in the post-intervention period when compared to pre-intervention, representing a reduction in bed-days and excess bed-days of 31.0 (104.6; p<0.001) and 15.0 (73.4; p=0.002) respectively. Outpatient visit frequency in the follow-up period decreased by an average of 10.6 appointments (42.2; p=0.001). No significant impact on A&E attendances was observed (mean 0.6; SD 9.3; p=0.26).
As the initial sample was imbalanced, with differential pre- and post-intervention observation windows, an additional analysis of 12-month resource utilisation pre- and post-intervention was conducted on pathways for those individuals with 12 months of observations available in both periods (window of analysis: 720 days; observations n=4,367; interventions n=129). Again, the results largely suggest reductions in resource utilisation in the post-intervention period versus pre-intervention. Excess bed-days decreased significantly by an average of 12.3 in the follow-up period (SD 48.0; p=0.01). Inpatient admissions and bed-days decreased ((mean reduction; SD; p-value) (0.5; 5.2; 0.19) and (20.4; 57.4; 0.25), respectively), although neither of these was statistically significant. A&E attendances increased (mean increase 0.4; SD 2.4; p=0.5) once again insignificantly. Outpatient attendances did decrease significantly, but the average reduction was negligible (mean reduction 0.01; SD 15.5; p=0.02).
Conclusions
This is the first analysis of a larger study intended to understand the effectiveness of Strattice™ RTM in ‘real-world’ major surgery. The sample exhibits substantial clinical heterogeneity, which may limit the interpretability and generalisability of the results. However, the results of this work support the proposition that abdominal surgeries employing biological mesh result in decreased secondary healthcare utilisation.
